items.q: (A) No sooner the rain had stopped than the players (B) ran back onto the pitch, (C) eager to finish the match (D) before darkness fell.
options: No sooner the rain had stopped
items.correction: No sooner had the rain stopped
items.explanation: After a negative adverbial such as No sooner at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary and subject invert: No sooner had the rain stopped than….

items.q: The head teacher (A) insisted that every pupil (B) wears a helmet on the cycling trip, (C) however short the route (D) turned out to be.
items.correction: wear a helmet
items.explanation: After verbs of demand such as insist, suggest, demand, the that-clause takes the subjunctive (base form): insisted that every pupil wear.

items.q: (A) Walking along the cliff path, (B) the lighthouse came into view, (C) its white tower (D) gleaming against the grey sky.
items.correction: we saw the lighthouse
items.explanation: A dangling modifier: the participle clause Walking along the cliff path must describe the subject of the main clause, and a lighthouse cannot walk, so the subject has to be the people walking.

items.q: If the council (A) had not raised the sea wall (B) back in the nineties, (C) the harbour would have been under water (D) at every high tide now.
options: had not raised the sea wall
the harbour would have been under water
items.correction: the harbour would be under water
items.explanation: A mixed conditional pairs a past condition (had not raised) with a present result marked by now, so the main clause needs would be, not the past-result form would have been.

items.q: If only I (A) listened to the guide's warning (B) about the tide, we (C) would not have spent the night (D) stranded on the rocks.
options: would not have spent the night
items.correction: had listened to the guide's warning
items.explanation: If only expressing regret about a past event takes the past perfect, matching the past-result clause would not have spent.

items.q: (A) It was not until the final whistle (B) when the exhausted goalkeeper (C) realised that she had kept (D) a clean sheet all season.
options: It was not until the final whistle
items.correction: that the exhausted goalkeeper
items.explanation: The cleft structure It was not until … that … requires that to introduce the second part, not when.

items.q: The museum guide told us (A) that the medieval scribes (B) had used surprisingly (C) few equipment to produce (D) such intricate manuscripts.
items.correction: little equipment to produce
items.explanation: Equipment is uncountable, so it takes little; few is only used with plural countable nouns.

items.q: The physics lecture (A) covered the theory of relativity (B) at such speed that (C) even the strongest students (D) left with so a vague understanding.
options: left with so a vague understanding
items.correction: left with such a vague understanding
items.explanation: Before a/an + adjective + noun the intensifier is such (such a vague understanding); so can only go directly before an adjective or adverb.

items.q: (A) Scarcely the plane had left the runway (B) when the passenger beside me (C) began describing every crash (D) he had ever read about.
options: Scarcely the plane had left the runway
items.correction: Scarcely had the plane left the runway
items.explanation: When Scarcely opens the sentence, subject and auxiliary invert: Scarcely had the plane left … when ….

items.q: (A) Despite the bakery opens at six, there is (B) always a queue stretching (C) around the corner (D) by half past five.
options: Despite the bakery opens at six
items.correction: Although the bakery opens at six
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and cannot be followed by a full clause with a finite verb; a clause needs the conjunction although (or despite the fact that).

items.q: The northern provinces (A) receive heavy monsoon rain (B) throughout the summer, whereas (C) the south it stays (D) largely dry until October.
items.correction: the south stays
items.explanation: A clause cannot have both a noun subject and a pronoun subject repeating it; the south stays already has its subject, so the extra it must go.

items.q: The new coach (A) expects every player (B) to arrive early, (C) to train hard, and (D) showing respect to the referee.
items.correction: to show respect to the referee
items.explanation: Items in a list must be parallel: after to arrive and to train, the third item must also be a to-infinitive, to show.

items.q: After months of secret talks, the two rival companies (A) finally signed a deal, (B) doing a compromise (C) on the price of the shared (D) patent licence.
options: on the price of the shared
items.correction: reaching a compromise
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with compromise is reach (or strike), never do.

items.q: The documentary (A) sheds light on how (B) migrating whales (C) make the most from ocean currents (D) to save energy on their journey south.
options: make the most from ocean currents
to save energy on their journey south
items.correction: make the most of ocean currents
items.explanation: The fixed expression is make the most of something; the preposition of cannot be replaced by from.

items.q: (A) Been badly injured in the first half, the captain (B) was carried off (C) on a stretcher while the crowd (D) fell silent.
options: Been badly injured in the first half
on a stretcher while the crowd
items.correction: Having been badly injured in the first half
items.explanation: A perfect passive participle clause needs Having been + past participle; the bare past participle been cannot open a participle clause on its own.

items.q: The residents (A) marched to the town hall and (B) demanded that the mayor (C) explains why the promised playground (D) had never been built.
options: marched to the town hall and
items.correction: explain why the promised playground
items.explanation: Demand that is followed by the subjunctive base form, so the third-person verb has no -s: demanded that the mayor explain.

items.q: Only after the last guest (A) had left (B) did we noticed that (C) the birthday cake was still (D) sitting untouched in the fridge.
items.correction: did we notice that
items.explanation: In the inverted structure after Only after…, the auxiliary did already carries the past tense, so the main verb stays in the base form: did we notice.

items.q: Not only (A) did the storm tear (B) the roof off the barn, (C) but it also (D) was flooding the entire lower field within an hour.
options: was flooding the entire lower field within an hour
items.correction: flooded the entire lower field within an hour
items.explanation: A completed past event, especially one measured by within an hour, takes the past simple flooded, matching did … tear in the first half; the past continuous wrongly presents it as unfinished.

items.q: If Marco (A) were a little more patient with his little cousins, they (B) would not hide his phone yesterday and he would not (C) be searching for it (D) now.
options: were a little more patient with his little cousins
would not hide his phone yesterday
items.correction: would not have hidden his phone yesterday
items.explanation: In a mixed conditional a present condition (were) can have a past result, but that past result marked by yesterday must use would have + past participle.

items.q: (A) After tasting the soup, (B) more salt was added by the chef (C) before the bowls were carried (D) out to the waiting diners.
options: more salt was added by the chef
items.correction: the chef added more salt
items.explanation: The participle clause After tasting the soup dangles: its implied subject (the chef) must be the subject of the main clause, so the passive more salt was added has to become active.

items.q: For most tourists, (A) climbing the volcano at dawn (B) proves far more memorable (C) than to watch the sunrise (D) from the hotel balcony.
items.correction: than watching the sunrise
items.explanation: The two things compared must have the same form: the gerund climbing must be balanced by the gerund watching, not a to-infinitive.

items.q: (A) A large amount of volunteers (B) turned up to plant mangroves (C) along the estuary, (D) far more than the organisers had catered for.
options: far more than the organisers had catered for
items.correction: A large number of volunteers
items.explanation: Volunteers is a plural countable noun, so the quantifier is a large number of; amount is reserved for uncountable nouns.

items.q: The chef's new tasting menu (A) has attracted (B) so many praise from critics that (C) tables are booked (D) up to three months in advance.
options: so many praise from critics that
up to three months in advance
items.correction: so much praise from critics that
items.explanation: Praise is uncountable, so the so … that structure needs so much; so many requires a plural noun.

items.q: Hardly (A) had the teacher handed out the papers (B) and told everyone (C) to begin writing (D) than the fire alarm went off.
options: had the teacher handed out the papers
than the fire alarm went off
items.correction: when the fire alarm went off
items.explanation: Hardly … when is the fixed pair; than belongs only with No sooner … than.

items.q: (A) What surprises me most about the desert are (B) how quickly the temperature drops (C) once the sun (D) has gone down.
options: What surprises me most about the desert are
items.correction: What surprises me most about the desert is
items.explanation: In a what-cleft the subject is the whole clause What surprises me most, which is singular, and the complement here is a clause, so the verb must be is.

items.q: The exhibition features (A) a set of portraits, (B) the largest of (C) them measures (D) nearly four metres across.
items.correction: which measures
items.explanation: Two finite clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; the second clause must be a relative clause with the largest of which, not the pronoun them.

items.q: The reporter (A) asked the marathon winner (B) whether she (C) had expected to break the record and (D) what was her next goal.
options: had expected to break the record and
items.correction: what her next goal was
items.explanation: A reported question keeps statement word order (subject before verb): what her next goal was, not the direct-question order what was her next goal.

items.q: (A) The expedition pressed on towards the summit (B) although the worsening weather, (C) reaching the ridge (D) just as the blizzard closed in.
options: The expedition pressed on towards the summit
just as the blizzard closed in
items.correction: despite the worsening weather
items.explanation: Although is a conjunction and must introduce a clause with a verb; before a noun phrase like the worsening weather the preposition despite (or in spite of) is required.

items.q: (A) Had been the ferry company warned about the storm earlier, it (B) would have cancelled the crossing (C) and the passengers (D) would have stayed ashore.
options: Had been the ferry company warned about the storm earlier
items.correction: Had the ferry company been warned about the storm earlier
items.explanation: In an inverted third conditional only the auxiliary had moves in front of the subject; been stays after it: Had the ferry company been warned….

items.q: Little (A) did the villagers suspect (B) that the quiet stranger (C) whom had bought the old mill (D) was a celebrated painter in hiding.
options: whom had bought the old mill
was a celebrated painter in hiding
items.correction: who had bought the old mill
items.explanation: The relative pronoun is the subject of had bought, so it must be the subject form who; whom is only used as an object.

items.q: The scandal (A) made serious damage to the minister's reputation, (B) and he was forced to (C) make a public apology (D) within days.
options: made serious damage to the minister's reputation
items.correction: did serious damage to the minister's reputation
items.explanation: Damage collocates with do (or cause), never with make, whereas make an apology in segment C is the correct pairing.

items.q: The committee (A) has agreed to (B) put off with the decision (C) until the full report (D) has been circulated to every member.
options: has been circulated to every member
items.correction: put off the decision
items.explanation: The phrasal verb put off (postpone) takes a direct object with no further preposition; with is intrusive.

items.q: The rapid (A) expansion of the city's metro network (B) has led to (C) a noticeable reduce in traffic (D) on the main ring road.
options: expansion of the city's metro network
items.correction: a noticeable reduction in traffic
items.explanation: After the article and adjective a noticeable a noun is needed, so the verb reduce must be nominalised to reduction.

items.q: Throughout the winter the charity (A) provides hot meals (B) in the station car park, (C) regardless of the weather, (D) for homeless and anyone else in need.
options: for homeless and anyone else in need
items.correction: for the homeless and anyone else in need
items.explanation: An adjective used to name a whole group of people takes the definite article: the homeless, like the elderly or the unemployed.

items.q: Neither the head chef (A) nor the two apprentices (B) who worked beside him (C) last night (D) was able to explain how the sauce curdled.
options: was able to explain how the sauce curdled
items.correction: were able to explain how the sauce curdled
items.explanation: With neither … nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the plural two apprentices, so it must be were.

items.q: Looking at the old photographs, (A) my father admitted (B) that he (C) wished he would have travelled more (D) before settling down.
options: wished he would have travelled more
items.correction: wished he had travelled more
items.explanation: Regret about the past after wish is expressed with the past perfect (wished he had travelled); would have is not used in the wish clause.

items.q: The twins (A) argued for an hour about (B) whose turn it was to walk the dog, (C) each insisting that (D) each other had walked him less this week.
options: whose turn it was to walk the dog
each other had walked him less this week
items.correction: the other had walked him less this week
items.explanation: Each other is a reciprocal object pronoun and can never be the subject of a clause; with each already in play, the subject must be the other.

items.q: By the time the new bridge (A) will open next spring, the ferry (B) will have carried commuters (C) across the river (D) for almost ninety years.
items.correction: opens next spring
items.explanation: A time clause introduced by by the time takes the present simple for future reference; will belongs only in the main clause (will have carried).

items.q: I (A) would rather you (B) didn't mention the surprise party (C) to my aunt, (D) whom tends to let secrets slip.
options: whom tends to let secrets slip
items.correction: who tends to let secrets slip
items.explanation: The relative pronoun is the subject of tends, so it must be who; whom is the object form and cannot be followed directly by a verb it governs.

items.q: It was (A) such a foggy morning (B) that the pilot (C) had no choice but (D) delaying the take-off by two hours.
options: delaying the take-off by two hours
items.correction: to delay the take-off by two hours
items.explanation: The expression have no choice but is followed by a to-infinitive (but to delay), not a gerund.
